h1: The 6 Best Dual-Basket Air Fryers of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Dual-Basket Air Fryers: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six dual-basket air fryers compared on capacity, Sync Finish and Match Cook modes, presets and price band for family meals.
summary: The Ninja DZ201 8 quart is the best dual-basket air fryer for most households, with Match Cook, Smart Finish and a 6-in-1 mode set. The DZ401 suits larger families, and the DZ550 adds a cook thermometer. The DoubleStack XL saves width, the Chefman is the budget pick and the Gourmia gives 10 quarts for less.
intro: A dual-basket air fryer earns its counter space only if you regularly cook two different foods at once. Shoppers compare total quarts, then discover that a 10 quart label means two baskets of roughly five, which will not hold a whole chicken or a full tray of wings. The numbers worth reading are the per-basket size and the sync feature that lets two foods finish together.

We reviewed eight models and ranked six on capacity, finish-together features, presets and price band. The ranking uses the spec sheets only, so it says nothing about how crisp the food comes out. Pick the size for your household first, then check footprint, because several of these are wide enough to crowd a small kitchen.

products.name: Ninja DZ201 Foodi 8 Quart 6-in-1 DualZone 2-Basket Air Fryer
products.verdict: Two baskets, Match Cook and Smart Finish in an 8 quart body.
products.description:
The DZ201 is an 8 quart, 6-in-1 DualZone air fryer with two baskets, in the $100 to $200 band. Two features separate it from a fryer with a divider. Match Cook copies one basket's settings to the other, so both cook the same food at once for a bigger batch. Smart Finish times two foods to end together, so a protein and a side land on the plate hot at the same moment. It also roasts, broils and dehydrates.

It ranks first because it covers most households without the bulk of the 10 quart models. Each basket is roughly four quarts, enough for a protein in one and a side in the other.

It suits couples and families of three or four. The caveats are that a big family may outgrow it and that its wide body takes real counter room.
products.skipIf: You cook for six or more.

products.name: Ninja DZ401 Foodi 10 Quart 6-in-1 DualZone XL 2-Basket Air Fryer
products.verdict: A 10 quart version for family-sized meals.
products.description:
The DZ401 is the 10 quart DualZone XL with two baskets, Match Cook, Smart Finish and the same 6-in-1 mode set, including dehydrate, in the $100 to $200 band. The two extra quarts translate to roughly five quarts per basket, which is the difference between a tight fit and a comfortable batch of wings.

It places second because the added capacity helps bigger meals, yet it takes more counter space than the DZ201, and many households will never fill the extra room. The functions are identical, so you are paying in space, not in features.

It suits families that regularly cook for five or six. A couple will not use the added capacity. Measure your counter, because the XL body is wider than most appliance garages allow, and skip it if space is tight.

products.name: Ninja DZ550 Foodi 10 Quart 6-in-1 DualZone Smart XL Air Fryer
products.verdict: A built-in cook thermometer for perfect doneness.
products.description:
The DZ550 is a 10 quart, 6-in-1 Smart XL DualZone with a cook thermometer, Match and Finish modes and a dehydrate function, in the $100 to $200 band. A built-in thermometer ends guesswork on meat: instead of cutting into a chicken breast, you cook to a temperature and the unit finishes accordingly.

It ranks third because the thermometer is the only upgrade over the DZ401, and that matters mostly for roasts and steaks. For fries and frozen foods it adds nothing, so the premium over the DZ401 is only worth paying if you cook meat often.

It suits cooks who roast chicken or steak and want a precise finish. Skip it if you mostly cook frozen foods, because the capacity and footprint match the DZ401 without the thermometer benefit.

products.name: Ninja Air Fryer DoubleStack XL
products.verdict: A 10 quart stacked design for narrower counters.
products.description:
The Ninja DoubleStack XL is a 10 quart, 6-in-1 model, SL401, in Deep Grey, in the $200 to $500 band. Its baskets are stacked rather than side by side, which narrows the footprint. A tall, narrow fryer fits on a counter where a wide DualZone would eat the work surface.

It ranks fourth because it costs a band more than the DZ401 for similar capacity, and the listing gives few details about sync features. You are paying to save width, not to cook better.

It suits kitchens where width is the limit, such as narrow galley counters or shared spaces. Skip it if budget matters most. A stacked layout also means one basket sits above the other, so check the height under your cabinets before you order.

products.name: CHEFMAN 6 Quart Dual Basket Air Fryer Oven with Easy View Windows
products.verdict: The cheapest dual-basket with viewing windows.
products.description:
The Chefman is a 6 quart digital double air fryer in black, with Easy View windows, Sync Finish, Hi-Fry and Auto Shutoff, in the $50 to $100 band. Easy View windows let you check browning without opening a basket and venting heat, which suits foods that go from golden to burnt quickly.

It ranks fifth because 6 quarts is the smallest capacity here, and it has fewer cooking modes than the Ninjas. It is the cheapest way to cook two foods at once with a finish-together feature, which is the entire point of a dual basket.

It suits singles and couples. Larger households will want a Ninja, since three-quart baskets limit batch size. Hi-Fry is a high-heat mode for crisping, but check the manual for the temperature it reaches.

products.name: Gourmia Dual Basket Air Fryer - 10 Qt Large Capacity
products.verdict: Ten quarts and seven presets at a lower cost.
products.description:
The Gourmia is a 10 quart dual-basket fryer with FryForce360 airflow, a digital display with seven presets and roast and bake functions, in the $50 to $100 band. Ten quarts at that price is rare, and the presets cover common foods without menu hunting.

It ranks last because the listing does not name a sync feature, which the Ninjas and Chefman do. Without a stated finish-together mode, you manage timers by hand when two foods need different durations, which defeats the main reason to buy two baskets.

It suits budget buyers who want room more than synchronized cooking. Skip it if you want two foods to finish together. Check the product page for sync wording before ordering, since an unnamed feature may simply be missing from the listing.

whatMatters.detail: Total quarts split between two baskets, so each basket is roughly half. A 10 quart model gives about 5 per side. That decides whether wings or a whole fish fit. Look for per-basket details or photos, and compare them to the largest item you cook regularly, since a basket that cannot take it makes the second one pointless.

Sync features time two foods so they end together even when cook times differ. Without it, you manage timers by hand. Look for Smart Finish or Sync Finish in the title, as on the Ninja models and the Chefman. A fryer with no named sync, like the Gourmia, leaves the juggling to you, and a mistimed side goes cold while the main finishes.

Match Cook copies one basket's settings to the other so both cook the same food, useful for big batches of fries or wings. It is separate from finish syncing. Check that it is listed, as on the DZ201, DZ401 and DZ550, and ask whether the baskets can be controlled independently too, since that is the real advantage of two zones.

Side-by-side baskets are wide and use counter depth, while stacked designs are narrower and taller. Measure your counter and the clearance under cabinets before buying. The Ninja DoubleStack XL is the stacked option here, and the DualZone models are wide, so leave room around the vents for heat to escape.

A cook thermometer or viewing window adds control, and each matters for a different job. The thermometer helps with meat, and windows let you watch browning without opening a basket. Decide if you will use them, because both raise the price. The DZ550 has a thermometer, and the Chefman has windows. Pick the one that matches the food you cook most.

faq.q: Do both baskets cook at different temperatures?
faq.a: Dual-basket models let each basket run its own setting, and sync features align finish times. Match Cook, by contrast, copies one basket's settings to the other for a larger batch of one food, which suits party platters.

For one or two people, yes, because a half-empty basket wastes heat and counter room. The Chefman at 6 quarts suits them better, with smaller baskets that are easier to fill and use less counter space. Ten quarts is more than most couples need.
For roasts, yes. The Ninja DZ550 includes one, so you cook meat to a temperature and avoid cutting into it to check, which keeps juices in. For fries and frozen foods, a thermometer adds nothing.

faq.q: How do I use Smart Finish?
faq.a: Set each basket's food and time, and the Ninja starts the longer one first so both end together. The DZ201, DZ401 and DZ550 all use this, and the Chefman has Sync Finish.

faq.q: How do I clean the baskets?
faq.a: Wash with warm soapy water and a soft sponge after each use; check the manual for dishwasher safety. Avoid abrasive pads on nonstick baskets, and dry them fully before putting them back, since trapped moisture can dull the coating.

faq.q: Can I use only one basket?
faq.a: Yes. All the dual models here allow single-basket cooking, so you never lose the option, which helps when you only need one food. Use Match Cook or Smart Finish for two.

finalTake: Buy the Ninja DZ201 for a household of three or four, or the DZ401 for five or six. Choose the DZ550 if you roast meat, the DoubleStack XL when width is your limit, and the Chefman for one or two people. Look at per-basket size and sync features before total quarts.
